name: Albastini
description: Albastini is a sophisticated point-trick game from Tanzania, likely derived from the Portuguese game Bisca. It features unique rules such as a total absence of the follow-suit requirement and a bidding phase where players sacrifice cards to set the trump.

overview.description: Albastini is a sophisticated point-trick game from Tanzania, likely derived from the Portuguese game Bisca. It features unique rules such as a total absence of the follow-suit requirement and a bidding phase where players sacrifice cards to set the trump.

history.origins: Believed to have been introduced to East Africa by Portuguese sailors or traders, Albastini (corruption of 'Al-Bisca' or similar) evolved into a distinct Tanzanian game with localized terminology like 'Mrithi' and 'Ndoa'.
timeline: 16th-18th Century: Portuguese Bisca enters East African ports (Zanzibar, Dar es Salaam).
Late 20th Century: Formalized local rules documented in Tanzania.
2010s: Digital versions by local developers (like Augustino Mponzi) popularize it in the app stores.
history.cultural: Commonly played in 'vijiwe' (social meeting points) in Tanzania. Winning a trick is called 'Kula' (eating).
history.evolution: While Bisca required following suit or trumping in its Italian/Portuguese origins, Albastini dropped this constraint, allowing for deeper 'sacrifice' plays.

setup.players: 2, 3, or teams of 2 (4 players) or 3 (6 players).
setup.dealing: 5 cards dealt to each player. Remaining cards form the stock. Dealer is chosen by agreement.

rules.objective: Capture tricks containing high-value cards to surpass 60 points (out of 120 total).
rules.gameplay: 1. **Bidding (Otea)**: Dealer's opponents place one card face-up. This signifies their desire for that suit to be trumps. 2. **Trump Flip**: Dealer turns up the top card of the stock. This suit becomes trump. If an opponent bid that suit, they swap their bid card for the trump card. 3. **The Play**: Lead any card. Others play any card (no follow-suit requirement). 4. **Winning**: Highest trump wins. If no trump, highest card of the led suit wins. 5. **Drawing**: Winner 'eats' the trick, draws a new card from the stock first, then others draw. Lead next. 6. **Endings**: Play continues until stock and hands are empty.
keyRules: Card Values: Ace=11, 7=10, King=4, Jack=3, Queen=2. Total in deck = 120.
Ndoa (Marriage): When a 7 is captured by an Ace of the same suit.
Mrithi (Target): To avoid a double-loss, you must reach a minimum point threshold (10 for individuals, 20 for 4-player teams, 30 for 6-player teams).
No follow-suit requirement: You can play any card at any time.

strategy.basic: Don't waste your trumps early. Use low-value cards (6, 5, 4, 3) to probe your opponents and safe-guard your points.
strategy.intermediate: Strategic Passing: Since you don't have to follow suit, use your point-cards (Ace/7) to win tricks that contain high-value discards from your partner.
strategy.advanced: Card Counting: There are only 36 cards. If you track the fallen 10s and face cards, you can calculate precisely when it's safe to drop your 7s.
tips: The '7' is the second highest card in Albastini—it is extremely valuable and should be protected/hunted.
Always try to win the second-to-last trick to draw the face-up trump card.

variations.name: Six Player Albastini
variations.description: Two teams of three. Requires reaching 30 points (Mrithi) to avoid the double-loss.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Six-player team format only adjusts point thresholds described in rules, so no separate engine overrides are needed.

scoring.description: Scoring is based on the total 120 card points and 'Victory Points' (VP).
scoring.winCondition: The side with >60 card points wins the hand.

synthesis.shortDescription: Tanzania's favorite trick-taking challenge. With 36 cards and no rules on following suits, tactical sacrifices and high-point captures are the path to victory.

hero.title: ALBASTINI
hero.subtitle: The Queen of Tanzanian Cards
hero.tagline: Follow no suits, follow only your strategy.
